title: Application
html:
Application 1: Production of High-Value-Added Bacterial Cellulose

Background

Bacterial cellulose (BC) is a form of cellulose produced by microorganisms such as acetic acid bacteria. Owing to its high purity, excellent water-retention capacity, superior mechanical strength, and biocompatibility, BC holds great promise for a wide range of applications, including wound dressings, medical materials, filters, and flexible materials.

The physical properties and functions of BC depend not only on the chemical properties of cellulose itself but also on its hierarchical structure, including the orientation and arrangement of cellulose fibers. In particular, aligning fibers in a specific direction may enable the targeted enhancement of mechanical properties, such as strength and flexibility. Therefore, the ability to manipulate fiber orientation and higher-order structures could unlock the full potential of BC and enable the design of materials with properties tailored to specific applications.

However, precisely controlling the structure of cellulose fibers at the macroscopic scale remains a significant technical challenge. Rather than modifying the structure after BC has been produced, we have focused on an alternative approach: controlling the spatial arrangement of the bacteria that produce cellulose, thereby regulating its structure during the production process itself.

Our Approach

We aim to fundamentally control the structure of BC by manipulating the spatial arrangement of the cellulose-producing bacteria themselves. Unlike conventional approaches that modify BC after its formation, our strategy seeks to achieve more direct and precise structural control by designing the arrangement of bacteria at the source of cellulose production.

Specifically, our project, “One Direction,” aims to create topological structures with defined directionality. This approach could make it possible to control the orientation and arrangement of cellulose fibers produced by individual bacteria according to their alignment. By promoting fiber alignment and bundling, we expect to improve the mechanical properties and structural stability of BC.

Potential Impact (or Future Perspectives)

In the future, we envision extending this linearization technology to various cellulose-producing microorganisms, potentially enabling the development of high-performance BC with tailored fiber architectures. Specific applications include tissue-engineering scaffolds for nerve and muscle regeneration, where high mechanical strength and specific fiber orientations are desirable; wound dressings and artificial blood vessels, where water resistance and biocompatibility are important; and environmentally friendly products such as straws, which require high strength and complete biodegradability.

Through this approach, we aim to create novel materials that combine distinctive structures and functionalities by controlling BC architecture from the spatial arrangement of its producing cells, opening up new possibilities for high-value-added applications beyond conventional BC materials.
